title: Linear Programming
subject: Mathematics
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: What is a Linear Programming Problem (LPP)?
cards.a: An optimization problem of maximizing or minimizing a linear objective function subject to a set of linear inequality constraints and non-negativity restrictions.
cards.hint: All variables and constraints must be strictly linear (degree 1).

cards.q: What is the Objective Function Z and Decision Variables?
cards.a:
Objective Function: Z = ax + by (the linear function to be maximized or minimized).
Decision Variables: x and y, representing the quantities to be decided (x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0).
cards.hint: Non-negativity restrictions x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 confine the problem to the First Quadrant.

cards.q: What is the Feasible Region in an LPP?
cards.a: The common region determined by the intersection of all given constraints including the non-negativity restrictions x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
cards.hint: Every point in the feasible region is a feasible solution to the LPP.

cards.q: What is a Convex Set and why is it important in LPP?
cards.a: A set of points where the line segment joining any two points in the set lies entirely within the set. The feasible region of every LPP is always a convex polygon.
cards.hint: Because the feasible region is convex, optimal solutions always occur on its boundary/vertices.

cards.q: State the Corner Point Theorem (Fundamental Theorem of LPP).
cards.a: The optimal value (maximum or minimum) of the objective function Z = ax + by, if it exists, occurs at one of the corner points (vertices) of the feasible region.
cards.hint: You only need to calculate Z at the vertices, never inside the interior!

cards.q: What is a Bounded vs Unbounded Feasible Region?
cards.a:
Bounded: The feasible region can be enclosed within a circle of finite radius (finite boundary on all sides).
Unbounded: The region extends infinitely in at least one direction.
cards.hint: A bounded region always possesses BOTH a maximum and a minimum value of Z.

cards.q: Condition for an optimal maximum value M to exist in an UNBOUNDED feasible region?
cards.a: M is the maximum of Z iff the open half-plane ax + by > M has NO points in common with the feasible region.
cards.hint: If ax + by > M shares even one point with the feasible region, Z has no finite maximum (unbounded solution).

cards.q: Condition for an optimal minimum value m to exist in an UNBOUNDED feasible region?
cards.a: m is the minimum of Z iff the open half-plane ax + by < m has NO points in common with the feasible region.
cards.hint: Board exam favorite: draw the dotted line ax + by = m and check if it intersects the shaded region.

cards.q: When does an LPP have Multiple (Infinitely Many) Optimal Solutions?
cards.a: When the objective function Z attains the optimal value at TWO adjacent corner points. Then every point on the line segment joining them is also an optimal solution.
cards.hint: Condition: The objective line ax + by = k is parallel to one of the boundary constraint lines.

cards.q: What is an Infeasible LPP (No Feasible Solution)?
cards.a: A situation where no single point satisfies all the given constraints and non-negativity restrictions simultaneously (the feasible region is empty / null set).
cards.hint: Example: x + y ≤ 1 and x + y ≥ 3 with x, y ≥ 0 cannot have any common point.

cards.q: What is an Unbounded Solution in LPP?
cards.a: When the objective function value can increase (or decrease) indefinitely to infinity without violating any constraints.
cards.hint: No finite maximum value exists for an unbounded solution.

cards.q: What is a Redundant Constraint?
cards.a: A constraint that does not affect or reduce the feasible region. Removing it leaves the feasible region completely unchanged.
cards.hint: Example: x ≥ 0, x ≥ -2. Here x ≥ -2 is redundant because x ≥ 0 is strictly stronger.

cards.q: Graphing inequality ax + by ≤ c: How to determine the correct half-plane?
cards.a: Test the origin (0, 0): if 0 ≤ c is true, shade the half-plane containing (0, 0). If false, shade the half-plane opposite to (0, 0).
cards.hint: Trap: If the line passes through (0, 0) (i.e. c = 0), test another point like (1, 0) or (0, 1) instead!

cards.q: Solid line vs Dotted (dashed) line in inequality graphs?
cards.a:
Use a solid line for non-strict inequalities (≤ or ≥) because boundary points are included.
Use a dotted line for strict inequalities (< or >).
cards.hint: In HSC standard LPP, constraints are always non-strict (≤, ≥), hence drawn with solid lines.

cards.q: MHT-CET shortcut for translating word problem constraints: 'at least' vs 'at most'?
cards.a:
'At least k' means ≥ k (minimum k).
'At most k' means ≤ k (maximum k).
'Not more than k' means ≤ k.
'Not less than k' means ≥ k.
cards.hint: Reversing these inequalities is the most common student error in word problem formulation.

cards.q: Relation between Minimizing Z and Maximizing -Z?
cards.a: Minimizing Z = Maximizing (-Z), and Min(Z) = - Max(-Z).
cards.hint: Useful when converting a minimization LPP to a maximization problem.

cards.q: What is the Iso-profit / Iso-cost Line Method?
cards.a: Assign an arbitrary value k to Z (ax + by = k). Move this line parallel to itself in the direction of increasing/decreasing k across the feasible region.
cards.hint: The last corner point touched by the line before leaving the feasible region is the optimal vertex.

cards.q: Can the optimal value of an LPP occur at an interior point of the feasible region?
cards.a: NO, never for a linear objective function. The optimal value always occurs on the boundary, specifically at a vertex.
cards.hint: A non-vertex point can be optimal only if all points on that boundary edge share the same optimal value.

cards.q: Maximum number of corner points for an LPP with n linear inequality constraints?
cards.a: At most ⁿC₂ intersection points of lines in the first quadrant.
cards.hint: Only those intersection points that satisfy all other inequalities qualify as feasible corner points.

cards.q: What is the value of Z = ax + by at the origin (0, 0)?
cards.hint: If a, b > 0 and (0,0) is in the feasible region, Z_min is usually 0 at (0, 0).

cards.q: What is Degeneracy in LPP?
cards.a: When more than two constraint lines pass through the exact same corner point (vertex) of the feasible region.
cards.hint: The corner point is over-determined by redundant constraint boundaries.

cards.q: Step-by-step Corner Point Method for HSC Board 4-mark questions?
cards.a:
1. Convert inequalities to equalities and find x/y intercepts.
2. Plot lines and shade feasible region using test points.
3. Determine all corner points (vertices) by solving line intersections.
4. Tabulate Z at every vertex; identify maximum / minimum.
cards.hint: A complete table of vertices with corresponding Z values is mandatory for full step marks.

cards.q: MHT-CET 15-second shortcut for corner point evaluation?
cards.a: First eliminate options where coordinates have negative values. Next, substitute the given option vertices directly into Z and select the extremum that satisfies all constraints.
cards.hint: Working backwards from options saves plotting time in entrance exams.

cards.q: Can an LPP have a feasible region that is a single point?
cards.a: YES. If the lines intersect at only one point that satisfies all inequalities, the feasible region is that single point, which is also the trivial optimal solution.
cards.hint: Example: x + y ≤ 2, x + y ≥ 2, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 reduces to the line segment x + y = 2.

cards.q: If constraints are x + 2y ≤ 10, 3x + y ≤ 15, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, what are the vertices of the feasible region?
cards.hint: Intersection of x + 2y = 10 and 3x + y = 15 gives x = 4, y = 3. Check (4, 3) satisfies both!
